lesson.title: Copy a message one base at a time

steps.headline: A DNA strand is a row of bases, and each base pairs with only one partner.

lead.text: A strand is a row of four kinds of base: A, T, C and G. A always pairs with T, and C always pairs with G.
So one strand fixes the other. Each strand is a template for its complementary partner.

steps.headline: Write the partner of the strand 5′-GATC-3′.

workedSteps.text: Pair each base with its partner.
Write the partners beneath, left to right.
The partner runs the opposite way along the molecule.
A pairs with T, so the first partner base is T.
Pair the rest, left to right.

steps.headline: Replication is semiconservative: each new molecule keeps one old strand.

lead.text: To copy DNA, the two strands separate. Each one acts as a template for a new partner.
Every new molecule is half old and half new.
Think of the unzipped strips again. After one round of copying, count the molecules that are zipped together.

reveal.text: You counted two molecules. Each took one old strand and built a new partner for it.

steps.headline: After copying, a chromosome is two joined copies. It is still one chromosome.

lead.text: A chromosome is one long DNA molecule with its proteins. Replication copies it.
The identical copies stay joined and are called sister chromatids. Together they count as one chromosome.
Copying has just happened in a cell. Its DNA amount has changed, but ask what has happened to the number of chromosomes.

reveal.text: The DNA doubled, but the chromosomes did not. Each one now has two sister chromatids.

lesson.orientation: Use complementary DNA bases and distinguish DNA amount from chromosome count.
lesson.reviewLabel: Copy a message one base at a time
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Two strips are zipped together. You unzip them, and give each loose strip a brand-new partner that fits it exactly.

intro.promise: By the end you'll copy a DNA strand base by base and say what each new molecule keeps.
intro.whyItMatters: Every new cell needs a complete copy of the instructions.

recap.keyIdea: Each strand of DNA is a template, so each new molecule keeps one old strand. Copying doubles the DNA but not the chromosome count.

blocks.text: You found the partner of two strands base by base, and counted two molecules from one.
You also kept the chromosome count at 4 while the DNA doubled.

recap.nextHook: Copied chromosomes are ready to be shared out. How does a cell make two cells?

questions.prompt: A new DNA base is placed opposite adenine (A). Give the name of its complementary base.
hints: The letters pair A with T, and C with G.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Adenine pairs with thymine in standard DNA base pairing.

questions.onCorrect: Thymine. A pairs with T, so the old strand decides which base comes next.

misconceptions.feedback: Those bases pair with each other, not with adenine.
Uracil is found in RNA. In DNA, adenine pairs with a different base.

questions.prompt: Write the partner bases beneath the strand 5′-AAGC-3′, from left to right.
hints: Pair one position at a time, keeping the same left-to-right order.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The aligned partner is 3′-TTCG-5′; the two strands run in opposite directions.

questions.onCorrect: TTCG. Each base takes its partner in turn, and the partner strand runs the opposite way.

misconceptions.feedback: That reverses the order. Keep the partner bases in step with the strand above.
That copies the strand itself. Write each base's partner.

questions.prompt: A double-stranded DNA molecule replicates once. How many double-stranded DNA molecules result?
hints: Separate strands serve as templates.
Each old strand receives a new partner.
Count the resulting paired molecules.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: One molecule is copied into two, each with one old and one new strand.

questions.onCorrect: 2. Each old strand gets a new partner, so one molecule gives two.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts strands. The question asks for double-stranded molecules.
The old strands each get a partner, which makes more than one molecule.

questions.prompt: A cell has 4 chromosomes before copying. Immediately after copying, while sister chromatids remain joined, how many chromosomes does it have?
hints: DNA amount and chromosome number are different counts.
Joined sister chromatids belong to one replicated chromosome.
Keep the chromosome count unchanged at this stage.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: It still has four chromosomes; each now has two sister chromatids.

questions.onCorrect: 4. Copying doubles the DNA but not the number of chromosomes.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts the chromatids. Joined chromatids still make one chromosome each.
Copying does not halve anything. The count stays as it was.

questions.prompt: What does semiconservative replication keep in each resulting DNA molecule?
hints: Trace the two original strands separately.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Each resulting molecule pairs an original template strand with a newly made strand.

questions.onCorrect: One original strand, paired with a new one. Each molecule is half old and half new.

misconceptions.feedback: The two original strands separate. Each ends up in a different molecule.
Every old strand is reused as a template, so each new molecule contains one.

questions.prompt: Six chromosomes each have two sister chromatids after copying. How many DNA molecules are present?
hints: Count both chromatids of each chromosome.
There are six replicated chromosomes.
Multiply the chromosomes by the chromatids in each.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each chromatid contains one DNA molecule: 6 × 2 = 12.

questions.onCorrect: 12. Each chromatid is one DNA molecule, and every chromosome now has two.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts chromosomes. Each one now holds two DNA molecules.
That is the chromatids in one chromosome. There are more chromosomes.

questions.prompt: An old strand reads ATGC. Write the bases of the new strand built against it, in the same left-to-right order.
hints: Pair each base in turn.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A pairs with T, T with A, G with C, and C with G, giving TACG.

questions.onCorrect: TACG. Each old base fixes its partner, so the new strand is fully determined.

misconceptions.feedback: That repeats the old strand. Write each base's partner.
That reverses the order. Keep the new bases in step with the old ones.

questions.prompt: A template strand has 40 bases. How many bases are in the new strand built against it?
hints: How many partners does each template base get?
Each base gets one partner.
The new strand is the same length as the template.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each template base gets exactly one partner, so the new strand also has 40 bases.

questions.onCorrect: 40. Every template base gets exactly one partner, so the strands match in length.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts both strands together. The question asks about the new strand only.
Nothing halves the length. Each template base still gets a partner.

questions.prompt: How many of the four strips in the new zipped pairs are brand new?
hints: The old strips are not thrown away. What happens to them?
Each old strip is given one new partner.
Count the new partners.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The two old strips are kept. Each gets one new partner, so two of the four strips are new.

questions.onCorrect: 2. Each pair keeps one old strip and gains one new one. DNA copying works the same way.

misconceptions.feedback: Two of the four are the old strips, which were kept.
Each old strip gets its own new partner, so there is more than one new strip.

questions.prompt: What makes a DNA strand a template?
hints: Think about what decides each new base.

acceptedIdeas: Its base order fixes the base order of its partner
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Because of base pairing, each base in the strand fixes the base opposite it.

choices.label: Its base order fixes the base order of its partner
It is always the longer strand
It can be read only from the left

questions.onCorrect: Its base order fixes its partner's. Each base allows only one partner.

misconceptions.feedback: Both strands are the same length. What matters is the order of their bases.
A strand can serve as a template at any point along its length.

questions.prompt: What are the two joined copies of a replicated chromosome called?
hints: The name includes a family relationship.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A replicated chromosome has two sister chromatids.

questions.onCorrect: Sister chromatids. They are identical copies that stay joined until the cell divides.

misconceptions.feedback: Homologous chromosomes come from different parents. These copies came from one chromosome.
